utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-84-R77.4, the Prosecutor versus Astrit Haraqija and Bajrush Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Haraqija, can you hear me in a language you understand? I do, however, not receive your answer. Your microphone is switched on? Yes. You're nodding, but nodding does not appear on the transcript, so --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haraqija. Mr. Morina, the same question for you. Do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm receiving interpretation in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then may have the appearances. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. David Re and Mr. Vincent Lunny. Our case manager is Axia Lecca --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem although the microphone is switched on I do not hear you properly, Mr. Re. Neither does the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you wish me to start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. David Re and Mr. Vincent Lunny and with case manager Axia Jahnsen Lecca for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Then for the Defence. The Defence for Mr. Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. If it please, Your Honour, Karim Khan for the first accused in this case Mr. Astrit Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Then for Mr. Morina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Mr. Jens Dieckmann from Germany for Mr. Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dieckmann. The -- we are here this afternoon at the initial appearance of you, Mr. Haraqija, and Mr. Morina. Later we'll invite you to enter a plea but I already note some details of the indictment. Mr. Haraqija, you are charged with one count of contempt of the Tribunal and in the alternative with incitement to contempt of the Tribunal pursuant to Rule 77 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And you, Mr. Morina, you're charged with one count of contempt of the Tribunal pursuant to Rule 77 of the Rules. That's what we are here for. The President of this Tribunal has ordered, on the 13th of February, 2008, that this case should be assigned to Trial Chamber I, composed of myself being the Presiding Judge, Judge Van Den Wyngaert, and Judge Moloto. In an order dated the 15th of February, this year, I designated Judge Moloto as the Pre-Trial Judge, but since Judge Moloto is not here today I'm conducting this initial appearance. May I first verify, Mr. Khan and Mr. Dieckmann, you have been appointed as duty counsel? Yes, I see you both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: That's correct. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again nodding doesn't appear on the transcript. Are there any -- have you experienced any problems in getting access to your clients or is it going the usual way? If there's any problem, please address me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as my client is concerned, it's going the usual way. We were informed yesterday that there would be an initial appearance today. We have both had the opportunity of spending about half an hour or so with our clients, maybe 45 minutes with our clients this morning. There's been nothing untoward in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dieckmann --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: I can support as well. It was excellent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the first thing I'd like to do is for the record, Mr. Haraqija, first to state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Astrit Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Haraqija, where were you born, and when?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 14th of June, 1972, in Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is your family aware of you being transferred to The Hague and detained at this moment in the United Nations Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, they are aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then Mr. Morina, same questions for you first. Could you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bajrush Morina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you were born where and when?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 10th of December, 1962, in Vjeda, Rahovec municipality in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I ask you whether your family is informed about your transfer to The Hague and your detention in the United Nations detention unit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they are informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you are assisted by counsel I don't think at this moment there is a need to read Article 20 and 21 of the statute which defines what rights you such as the right to remain silent and other rights. Counsel will inform you about that. If you have any questions about your rights, then you may ask them. My next question to you, fir, Mr. Haraqija, have you received the indictment in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you understand the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to discuss your indictment with counsel, with Mr. Khan?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we discussed it this morning for around 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Morina, you -- have you received the indictment in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you understand the content of the indictment that was brought against you in.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to discuss the content of the indictment with Mr. Dieckmann?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had a certain period of time, around 45 minutes, to discuss it with my lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am addressing now both of you, Mr. Haraqija, and Mr. Morina. You have the right, the indictment, to be read out in full. Do you wish to exercise that right or would you refrain from having it read out in full? Of course I'll come to the individual counts at a later stage, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may assist. I have spoken to my client in relation to that. The indictment does not have to be read in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that you're nodding as a support, Mr. Haraqija. Mr. Morina, the same. I was addressing both of you. What is your answer as to whether you want to exercise the right to have the indictment read out in full or to waive that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that wouldn't be necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Pursuant to Rule 62(A)(iii) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal you have the right to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on each count today, or if you wish so, within 30 days from this initial appearance. On the basis of your discussions you had with counsel and also in view of whether you consider them sufficient at this moment, do you wish to enter a plea today, or would you rather use your right to enter a plea within the 30 days to come? Mr. Haraqija.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I plea not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll come to that later, but I do understand that you want to enter a plea today and not at any later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would prefer to enter a plea today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Morina, as far as you are concerned, do you want to enter a plea today or within the next 30 days?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would prefer today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Haraqija, may I invite you to stand. Mr. Haraqija, you are charged with one count of having committed contempt of the Tribunal, punishable under the Tribunal's inherent power and Rule 77(A)(iv) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there is an alternative charge brought against you in the indictment. It is one count of incitement to contempt of the Tribunal punishable under the Tribunal's inherent power and Rule 77(A)(iv) and (B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. How do you plead to this second count, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same plea, Your Honour, not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, would you please put on the record that Mr. Haraqija has pleaded not guilty on the both alternative counts. Please be seated, Mr. Haraqija. Mr. Morina, would you please stand. Mr. Morina, you're charged with one count of having committed contempt of the Tribunal by -- which is punishable under the Tribunal's inherent power and Rule 77(A)(iv) of the rules. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Registrar I would like you to put on the record that Mr. Morina has pleaded not guilty to the count which was brought against him. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, accused Haraqija and Mr. Morina both plead not guilty to the counts alleged in the indictment. It's now recorded in the transcript and for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Registrar, the registry is instructed to fix a date for trial when appropriate. You will understand that we cannot immediately fix a date, but we'll do that in the near future. Yes, we'll fix the date in the near future. You both will remain in custody of this Tribunal, but you're entitled to file an application for provisional release pursuant to Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal. Your Defence counsel can assist you with it if you wish to make such an application. Then the next point I would like to raise is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps it's -- it would be efficient to raise at this point. I understand of course it's very early days and it's very difficult with Your Honour's very busy court schedule to have an indication as to when this matter is likely to come to trial. However, I wonder if an indication as to the approximate period that is likely could be given. The reason I mention it is that there has been very brief discussions with my friends from the Prosecution and apparently their view on provisional release is going to be very much affected by the timing of this trial. I understand if this matter comes up in the next four weeks they will oppose provisional release, but of course if it's somewhat later their view may be a little bit different. Of course my learned friends will speak for themselves, but I would just ask you Your Honours -- Your Honour that as soon as possible if the parties could be informed as to the approximate time scale as to when this matter is likely to come to trial. My client's brother is getting married on the 10th of May, and so we will be filing an application for provisional release on the usual grounds but also on the ground of humanitarian reasons but, Your Honour, an early indication would be most welcome. I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann, I take it you would like to join --

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We participated in the short discussions with our learned friends from the Prosecution, and I support the submissions here of my learned colleague, and we also would invite the Chamber to give us instructions about their estimate start of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it may assist it seems from the papers that this would be a very short matter, four or five days at most. It's a matter of course of squeezing it in an already jam-packed courtroom given all the other things that are going on here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not only a matter of court time. It's also you need three Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Of course. And that's one of the big difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And sometimes one is sitting in the morning, the other is sitting in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you have to find not only a courtroom but especially in this case I take it because of our translation. So it's a rather complex logistic exercise and that's what I can promise you where the Judges will be as flexible as possible. And as soon as we know more, and it might for us be also important if an application will be filed, as you said, for provisional release, it might be a matter to consider for the Chamber as well what granting or denying such an application would actually mean for the accused. So therefore it's a shared concern to find out as soon as possible when this case could be heard. Mr. Re, is there anything you'd like to add to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To make the Prosecution's position clear on that, yes, it is true that our response to any provisional release application does depend to some degree upon the length of any pre-trial adjournment or detention, that is in fact correct. I can't give you a figure at the moment because we have no idea when the trial could be heard, but the Prosecution's position is of a prima facie opposition to provisional release at the moment on the basis that these are very serious offences striking at the root of justice and the very heart of justice, and if the accused are convicted they would be facing a substantial custodial sentence inevitably one greater than that imposed in the other case of witness interference of three months. It would have to be longer than three months' detention -- imprisonment for an offence of wilfully interfering with a witness before the witness testifies mid-trial. And the case of course would be aggravated by the position of the accused Haraqija as a minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks as if you're already arguing why it should not be granted, Mr. Re, which at the moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At the moment yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which would be premature. At this moment we're just dealing with the procedural and the scheduling part of that. And of course the Chamber is also, to some respect, is also dependent on what the parties do. And may I take it that disclosure and whatever Defence counsel could think of doing might which might delay the start of the trial. So to that extent it's not only in the hands of the Chamber. But if you would like to express yourselves on such matters that you would not need more time. For example, if -- if the supporting material is disclosed to you and if you say I need eight weeks to study it, I doubt whether that would be -- it's not that extensive but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: No. Well, Your Honour, a file has just been passed to us, my learned friend and I, before Your Honour entered the courtroom. It's a very small, given the nature of these cases that one normally has, it's a very small discrete issue. It appears to be primarily predicated upon telephone intercept and the evidence of one witness in your last case, and perhaps one of the accused in this. It seems to be a discrete issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Saying that however, Your Honour, saying that however given the sentence, the maximum sentence that this offence could carry, the Defence would not think it very prudent to rush to trial without, of course, looking at the nature of the intercepts and doing their own investigations. So I don't see it likely that we would be ready in the next four weeks to go to a time given by my learned friend earlier out of courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, of course Mr. Re started already arguing, which was that there's a -- there's a penalty to be expected, which is of such duration that would such already justify to be very careful in deciding whether or not to grant provisional release. That's of course, as I said before, that's all a bit premature. But you're certainly aware that if you are insisting on more time that this could have consequences for the length of -- of the pre-trial detention if no provisional release would be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, certainly one doesn't require months to prepare this case. It's -- one would be sensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest that the parties and the Chamber staff would try to keep in touch and to identify all relevant elements in terms of when to start, to see what party the Prosecution would need, what Defence would need, and then to see what -- what would be feasible. I suggest, therefore, the problem is that I will be here this week. Next week I'll not be here, but then Judge Moloto, who is the Pre-Trial Judge will be back. So we will try to communicate in such a way that we find such a date as early as reasonable possible so that we have the case to be heard without undue delay. Mr. Khan, I take it that if you want to file an application for provisional release that you'll do it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The sooner you do it the better the chance that I at least can form an opinion about it, just me because the whole Chamber has to decide before I leave Saturday, this weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just add something? I'm not arguing the toss. There would -- it would certainly assist the Prosecution in formulating its response if we had some indication of when the trial would be likely to occur, and I emphasise Mr. Khan is quite correct. It's a very short trial. It's maybe three, four, five Prosecution witnesses depending upon agreements and a listening device, the contents of a listening device, a tape, and some interviews with the accused. The Prosecution is trial-ready in the sense that if we had to go to trial next week, subject to getting the witnesses, we could do so. There is no further investigatory work to be done. The case is absolutely ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that. I can promise you that the Judges will review their court schedules and see whether there are slots available to hear this case. The Chamber will be in communication with the registry to find out whether all the other elements we need to hear a case are there, and then of course finally if that results in anything, then we'll communicate with the parties as well what seems to be feasible, and we'll try to do that as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm most grateful. Perhaps I could beg your indulgence to make one request, simply out of a desire to comply with Your Honour's preference to have something filed before Your Honour leaves on Saturday, I'm not going to argue the substance of the provisional release application, but the information I have received is the Prosecution informed my client during the elections in Kosovo last year and then in January of this year as to the nature of the allegations. And secondly, on Friday of last week he was approached by an OTP employee in Pristina and told that he would be transferred on Monday. He went to the ICTY offices himself on Saturday -- sorry, on Sunday and surrendered his passport and voluntarily came in on Sunday -- on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Khan --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, all I'm asking for -- Your Honour all I'm asking for is a brief letter from the Prosecution verifying that. Of course it would be germane, the aspect of voluntary surrender, to the risk of flight and it would perhaps expedite a provisional release application so that this matter would not be contentious between the parties. It's a matter simply that I put on record in court so that it saves us to have to put a formal application to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think as a matter of fact there is no need for that. If you approach the Prosecution say, "This is what we want to put forward, is there any challenge to that?" And then next time you come in court or you just put it in your application.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that Mr. Re will --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if he agrees -- it sounds as if we have already some reasons why provisional release should not be granted on the record, as I said premature, and it sounds as if we also have now on the record already some arguments why provisional release better should be granted. So it's one to one now as far as premature arguing. Mr. Dieckmann, you're still at zero, if you'd like to change that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. We prefer to do it in writing and we will inform the Chamber about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's still one to one to zero. Then having dealt with this, I would like to know whether there are any health concerns as far as you are concerned, Mr. Haraqija or Mr. Morina, of which the Chamber should be aware of, and if there are any, and if you'd like to discuss them not in public, please tell me. Then we'll go into private session, and we would deal with any such concerns in private session. Mr. Haraqija, any health issues to be raised?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED HARAQIJA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm very well thank you. I haven't had no health problems, and I am young, so I will be able to deal with everything here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Morina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MORINA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am feeling very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. So there are no health issues. Is there any other matter either the Prosecution or the Defence would like to raise? Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just note that we -- as Mr. Khan said, we have provided the supporting material. The only other material we have to give, and we'll give it this afternoon, is the witness testimony at trial, and they'll get that as soon as we finish here, I think. So all disclosure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Disclosure under Rule 66 will be complete this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Except maybe some Albanian translations but they'll be very shortly coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dieckmann.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIECKMANN
utterances.text: Nothing for the Accused Mr. Morina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes this initial appearance. We stand adjourned sine die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 2.51 p.m. sine die. 25
